questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Urban sprawl and the density gradient
questions.learningObjective: Identify what urban sprawl describes in a density pattern
questions.stem: A city where population thins gradually from a dense core to a wide fringe is best described by which term?

options.text: Compact city, a dense urban form with limited outward expansion
options.misconception: names the opposite spatial pattern

options.text: Gentrification, the upgrading of housing in an existing inner neighbourhood
options.misconception: names a different process that renews rather than spreads

options.text: Suburbanisation, the shift of residents to outer residential districts
options.misconception: describes population shift rather than density pattern

options.text: Urban sprawl, the outward spread of low-density development beyond the core

questions.explanation: Urban sprawl names the outward, low-density expansion beyond the core. Gentrification and suburbanisation are related but distinct processes, and a compact city is the opposite form.
questions.hint: Look for the term about outward low-density spread.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Density decline with distance from the centre
questions.learningObjective: Explain why density falls as distance from the centre rises
questions.stem: Explain why residential density generally falls as distance from the city centre increases.

answer.exemplar: Land prices are highest near the centre, so developers build tall and dense there; farther out, cheaper land permits larger lots and lower density, producing a declining density gradient.

questions.explanation: High central land prices reward intensive use, while cheaper peripheral land allows larger lots. Together these forces create a smooth decline in density outward.
questions.hint: Connect land price to building intensity.

questions.topic: Implied density from population and footprint
questions.learningObjective: Compute density from population and land area
questions.stem: A district holds 45,000 people on a built-up footprint of 3 km2. What is the density in persons per km2?
questions.explanation: Density equals population divided by area: 45,000 / 3 = 15,000 persons per km2. The arithmetic is checked by multiplying back.

options.text: Subsidising large-lot housing on the periphery

questions.hint: Pick the managed-limit tool.

stimulus.body: Source note: Falling average density while population grows. This is the claim the evidence in the topic supports.

questions.stem: A document on urban sprawl and the density gradient reads: "Falling average density while population grows" Using that evidence, which indicator most clearly signals urban sprawl in a metro area?

options.text: Shorter average commute times
options.misconception: sprawl usually lengthens commutes

options.text: Rising density in the central business district
options.misconception: describes compaction, not sprawl

options.text: Falling average density while population grows
More transit riders per capita
options.misconception: sprawl usually lowers transit use

questions.explanation: Sprawl adds area faster than people, so average density falls even as population rises. The other options describe compaction or transit-rich forms.
questions.hint: Sprawl dilutes density as population grows.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Density decline with distance from the centre
questions.learningObjective: Compute the density at a named distance
questions.stem: A gradient falls linearly from 100 persons per hectare at 0 km to 20 at 10 km. In stage one, what is the density at 5 km?

options.text: 40 persons per hectare, a quarter of the range
options.misconception: misplaces the midpoint

options.text: 50 persons per hectare, half the centre value
options.misconception: halves the centre instead of interpolating

options.text: 80 persons per hectare, 20 below the centre
options.misconception: uses a 20 drop instead of 40

options.text: 60 persons per hectare, the midpoint of the two values

questions.explanation: Linear decline from 100 to 20 over 10 km gives 60 at 5 km, the midpoint. Halving or misplacing the drop gives the wrong value.
questions.hint: Take the midpoint of 100 and 20.

questions.stem: A 10 km radius city has density 100 persons per hectare in its inner 3 km2 and 25 persons per hectare in the remaining 7 km2. What is total population?
questions.explanation: Inner population is 100 x 300 = 30,000 and outer is 25 x 700 = 17,500, totalling 47,500. Areas are converted to hectares before multiplying.
questions.hint: Convert km2 to hectares before multiplying.

10,000 persons per km2

options.text: 2,500 persons per km2
options.misconception: divides area by population

questions.stem: Explain why raising the minimum lot size lowers the number of lots a site can yield.

answer.exemplar: A larger minimum means each lot consumes more land, so a fixed site produces fewer lots; this reduces density and can raise housing costs.

questions.explanation: Each lot takes more land, so fewer fit on a fixed site. Density falls and costs can rise. The exemplar grounds the answer in lot yield after a minimum lot size change rather than restating the question.
questions.hint: More land per lot means fewer lots.

options.text: Sprawl is a density pattern; suburbanisation is a population movement
